name: Physics
strapline: Understand the forces shaping our world.
intro: Use models, measurements and mathematics to explain motion, energy and technology. Suggested BGE projects need departmental review. National course content is separated from optional exploration. All physical investigations require teacher direction and school safety procedures; independent tasks here use supplied data, diagrams or simulations.

bge.title: Motion around Govan
bge.question: How can we describe a journey?
bge.task: Use a fictional bus timetable to calculate average speed between stops. Explain the assumptions.
bge.extend: Sketch why a journey’s average speed differs from its maximum speed.

bge.title: Powering our future
bge.question: Where does useful energy go?
bge.task: Draw an energy-transfer diagram for a lamp and explain the meaning of wasted energy.
bge.extend: Compare two lighting options using energy and lifetime data.

bge.title: Signals and sound
bge.question: How does information travel?
bge.task: Annotate a supplied wave diagram and write what would change for a higher-pitched sound.
bge.extend: Explain why sound cannot cross a vacuum.

bge.title: Space explorers
bge.question: What can light tell us about space?
learn: Use the idea of a light-year.
bge.task: Create a scale comparison from NASA data with units and an explanation of what is omitted.
bge.extend: Explain why seeing a distant galaxy means seeing its past.

senior.title: Physics
senior.explain: Build explanations through numerical work and enquiry. National 4 adds an investigation assignment.
senior.assessment: Internally assessed units, with added value at National 4; pass/fail.

senior.title: National 5 Physics
senior.explain: Connect six content areas through problem solving, experimental evidence, equations and units.
senior.assessment: Question paper and assignment. This hub’s calculations are practice examples, not live assignment responses.

senior.title: Higher Physics
senior.explain: Extend motion, gravitation, waves, particles, circuits and fields using mathematical models. Researching Physics supports enquiry.
senior.assessment: Question paper and assignment; use the current session specification.

skills.title: Select a relationship
skills.explain: List quantities, units and the unknown before choosing an equation.
skills.try: Find acceleration for velocity changing from 4 to 16 m s⁻¹ in 3 s.

skills.title: Read a circuit
skills.explain: Trace connected points, identifying series paths and parallel branches.
skills.try: Explain where a voltmeter measures the potential difference across a component.
skills.check: It connects in parallel; an ammeter measures current in series.

skills.title: Use a graph
skills.explain: Gradient represents change in the vertical quantity divided by change in the horizontal quantity.
skills.try: Explain the gradient of a velocity–time graph.
skills.check: It is acceleration, with units m s⁻²; area represents displacement.

skills.title: Evaluate measurement
skills.explain: Resolution, random variation and systematic effects influence results.
skills.try: Compare five repeated timings with one reading.
skills.check: Repeats help assess random variation; they do not automatically remove systematic error.

practice.question: A 12 V supply passes 0.50 A through a resistor. Calculate resistance and power.
practice.hint: Use V = IR and P = VI.
practice.answer: R = 12/0.50 = 24 Ω. P = 12 × 0.50 = 6.0 W. Include both units and show substitution.
practice.extend: Predict the current if voltage doubles and resistance stays constant.

practice.question: A wave has frequency 5 Hz and wavelength 2 m. What is its speed? Explain what frequency measures.
practice.answer: v = 5 × 2 = 10 m s⁻¹. Frequency is the number of complete oscillations per second, not the distance between peaks.
practice.extend: If speed stays constant and frequency doubles, calculate the new wavelength.

practice.question: Two identical balls are dropped from the same height; one experiences substantial air resistance. Must they arrive together?
practice.hint: Separate the ideal model from actual forces.
practice.answer: In the ideal no-air-resistance model, acceleration is the same. With substantial air resistance, net force and acceleration can differ, so arrival times need not match.
practice.extend: Explain which measurements could test whether air resistance matters.

resources.title: PhET simulations
resources.task: Explore Circuit Construction Kit virtually and record a prediction before changing a circuit.

resources.title: NASA learning resources
resources.task: Choose a space explanation and distinguish an observation from its interpretation.

resources.title: Institute of Physics
resources.task: Connect one physics story to a course concept and explain its relevance.

resources.title: Royal Institution films
resources.task: Find a physics talk and create three retrieval questions; do not reproduce demonstrations.

resources.title: Official past papers
resources.task: Attempt one calculation before revealing the official marking instructions.

ipad.title: Explain a graph
steps: Annotate three intervals with physical meaning.
Record a narrated explanation including units.
ipad.evidence: A labelled graph and a 60-second explanation.

ipad.title: Simulation investigation
steps: Capture three settings and record outcomes in a table.
State a trend and the limits of the model.
ipad.evidence: Screenshots support an explanation, rather than replace one.

ipad.title: Equation clinic
steps: Write a worked solution with quantities and units.
Use screen recording to explain each step.
Correct a deliberate unit error in a second example.
ipad.evidence: Two solutions showing reasoning and checking.

parentTip: Ask for a diagram explaining a familiar technology. Praise the use of units and evidence, and encourage questions when a model does not match the real world.

visual.title: Read a distance–time graph
visual.question: A person travels 20 m in 10 s, waits for 5 s, then travels another 20 m in 5 s. Which section has the greatest speed?
visual.answer: The final section: 20 m ÷ 5 s = 4 m/s. The first section is 2 m/s. The horizontal section represents no change in distance: the person is stationary.
